1. Can you provide an explicit justification for each component in the signature? Also, what is exactly the second component?


1. The first component gives a score of how much the prediction favored the misprediction compared to the true prediction.
2. The second component is the first order and second order derivative, which helps identify how much influence each feature has to the prediction, and how much the prediction difference changes with a unit change in feature or feature interaction.
3. The third component is to measure the contribution due to the feature value, i.e. the magnitude of the impact caused by a feature.


1. Do you have an example, constructed or from your experiments, that can demonstrate two failures with the same signature actually comes from the same failure region (i.e., they fail for the same reason)? -- I will try to plot an example for this one in a 2d space to visualize.

I agree, Dr. Lei. Decision signature is the key component.

It should be able to generate more information than the features alone. Also, our assumption is that a similar decision signature means a similar fix, which I’m a little doubtful with the current decision signature that I have.

I will provide more detailed response and examples to your questions after giving some thoughts.

Yes, Dr. Lei. for the evaluation, I’m following LEIA’s approach. They have three sets: train, val, test. They initially train a model using train set, they use the val set to perform the model fixing, and test the performance on the test set. So, there is no information leakage from the test set, as it is only used for final evaluation. Similarly for our approach, no information from the final set is used to improve the model.

I think, this ICLR 2025 paper is very related: [proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/…/fe96ca55e42f8087c4f2e3a06efc7ed1-Paper-Conference.pdf](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/fe96ca55e42f8087c4f2e3a06efc7ed1-Paper-Conference.pdf) regarding error discovery and model repair. I will read this in more detail as I prepare for the submission.
Sure, Dr. Lei. I will submit to ICLR.

Hi Dr. Lei, I have summarized below the approach submitted in our AAAI submission after addressing the initial concerns. I would appreciate any additional concerns or suggestions you may have.



1. Problem setup


We start with a trained classifier consisting of a frozen feature extractor and a linear classification head. The feature extractor maps each input to a learned feature representation, and the classification head converts that representation into class scores. (This is a same setup as the baseline approach, LEIA)

We use a small labeled repair set containing both correct predictions and failures. A failure occurs when the true class is a, but the classifier predicts class b; we denote this error direction as a → b.

Our key hypothesis is that failures arising from similar decision logic are more likely to benefit from the same correction. Because one global correction may help some failures while harming others, we discover separate failure regions and learn a correction for each region.

2. Decision-signature extraction

For each failure, we construct a decision signature that describes how the classifier favored the predicted class over the true class. The signature captures:


> the difference between the scores of the predicted and true classes;
> the rate of change and curvature of their pairwise probability with respect to that score difference; and
> the signed contribution of each learned feature to the incorrect class preference.

Here, the pairwise probability measures the classifier’s preference for the predicted class when comparing only the predicted and true classes.

Two failures may have the same error direction but different decision signatures because the classifier may rely on different learned features to produce the same type of error.

3. Failure-region discovery

We first separate failures by error direction. For example, all “cat predicted as dog” failures are considered separately from “cat predicted as bird” failures.

Within each error direction, we cluster failures that have similar decision signatures. Each resulting cluster becomes a failure region.

A failure region therefore contains examples with the same error direction and similar patterns of learned-feature contributions to the incorrect class preference. We use these patterns as an operational description of similar decision logic. Different failure regions within the same error direction may receive different corrections.

4. Anchored regional corrections

For each failure region, we learn one lightweight residual correction to the original class scores. The failures assigned to that region teach the correction which predictions should change.

We also train the correction using correctly predicted examples, which we call anchors. These anchors teach the correction which predictions should remain unchanged. Additional penalties keep the correction small and limit how much it changes the scores of correct examples.

Each regional correction is therefore trained to repair its assigned failures while preserving the classifier’s existing correct behavior.
